readerTitle: Dove's bet: say what every beauty ad left out
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Dove/Unilever, Campaign for Real Beauty, 2004~) + 가상 적용 (배관·수리 업체)
insight: 모든 경쟁자가 같은 약속을 할 때, 그 약속이 고객에게 남긴 불편함이 가장 큰 빈자리다.
misconception: 포지셔닝은 경쟁사보다 더 나은 제품 기능을 더 크게 외치는 것이다.

sources.text: Etcoff, N., Orbach, S., Scott, J., D'Agostino, H. (2004). The Real Truth About Beauty: A Global Report. Dove/Unilever 의뢰 연구 ("beautiful" 자기 묘사 2%)
Dove/Unilever 공식 자료: Campaign for Real Beauty 연혁 (2004 출범, Tick Box 광고, 2005 firming 광고, 2006 Evolution, 2013 Real Beauty Sketches)
Cannes Lions 2007 수상 기록 (Dove "Evolution" Grand Prix)
BBC, The Guardian 등 2017년 10월 Dove 페이스북 광고 사과 보도
Unilever 보도자료 (2020): Fair & Lovely를 Glow & Lovely로 개명

factChecks.note: 캠페인 출범 연도(2004)와 대행사(Ogilvy & Mather)를 Unilever 자료로 확인하세요. 카드에는 대행사 이름을 쓰지 않았습니다.
"2%만이 스스로를 아름답다고 표현"은 2004년 Real Truth About Beauty 보고서(10개국 약 3,200명 대상)의 널리 인용되는 수치입니다. 원문의 정확한 문구와 표본을 확인하세요.
Tick Box 광고 문구 예시 "Wrinkled? Wonderful?"가 실제 광고 문구와 일치하는지 확인하세요.
Evolution(2006)의 Cannes Lions 2007 Grand Prix 수상 부문(Film, Cyber)을 확인하세요. 카드에는 부문 없이 "top prizes at Cannes Lions"로 적었습니다.
매출 성장 수치(예: 10년간 25억→40억 달러 등)는 출처가 불확실해 카드에서 뺐습니다. 캠페인과 매출의 인과도 단정하지 않았습니다.
2017년 페이스북 바디워시 광고 논란과 사과, 2020년 Glow & Lovely 개명, Axe/Lynx 광고에 대한 비판은 게시 전 언론 보도로 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Dove's bet: say what every beauty ad left out
body: For decades, beauty ads showed the same face: young, thin and flawless.
In 2004, Dove, a Unilever brand best known for its soap bar, put ordinary women on billboards. Next to each photo were tick boxes, such as *Wrinkled? Wonderful?*, and passers-by were invited to vote.

image.label: Billboard of an older woman with two tick boxes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 도시 거리의 대형 빌보드에 미소 짓는 주름진 노년 여성 사진, 옆에 체크박스 두 개("Wrinkled?", "Wonderful?"). 지나가는 사람들이 올려다봄. 실제 Dove 로고, 제품 포장, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run the Dove brand team.
body: It's the early 2000s. You lead a brand team inside a giant consumer company. Every rival makes one promise: use this and look like the model.
Research your brand commissioned suggests very few women would describe themselves as beautiful. What's your next campaign?

options.text: Show the science of your moisturizing cream, with a top model
options.feedback: Safe and proven in the category. But it puts you in the same spot as every rival, competing on claims customers can barely tell apart.

options.text: Use real women of many ages and sizes, and question the beauty standard itself
options.feedback: It takes a position no rival holds and speaks to a feeling the research found. The cost: you now have to live up to that stance everywhere.

options.text: Sign a famous celebrity to make the brand feel aspirational
options.feedback: It can buy fast attention. It also deepens the very message your research says leaves customers feeling worse.

cards.title: It started with the 2%.
body: Dove commissioned a global study, *The Real Truth About Beauty* (2004). It was widely reported that only **2%** of women surveyed chose "beautiful" to describe themselves.

Dove built the Campaign for Real Beauty on that gap. Its ads used women of different ages, sizes and skin tones. In 2005, its firming lotion ads showed real women in plain underwear instead of models.
The message was not "our cream works better." It was "the standard is the problem."

cards.title: People shared it because it showed the trick.
body: In 2006, Dove released *Evolution*, a short film. In about a minute, an ordinary woman gets makeup, lighting and heavy digital retouching until she becomes a billboard face.

It spread widely online, back when online video was still new, and won top prizes at Cannes Lions in 2007. In 2013, *Real Beauty Sketches* had a forensic artist draw women from their own descriptions, then from strangers'. The strangers' portraits looked kinder.
Much of the attention was **earned**: people chose to share and argue about it.

image.label: A face changing from plain to retouched billboard
image.brief: 왼쪽에서 오른쪽으로 같은 여성 얼굴이 단계별로 변하는 가로 띠. 맨얼굴 → 메이크업 → 조명 → 포토샵 보정 커서 → 빌보드 속 완벽한 얼굴. 실제 광고 장면이나 로고를 그대로 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Positioning in the category's blind spot
body: **Positioning** is the place your brand holds in customers' minds, compared with the alternatives.

When every rival makes the same promise, that promise often leaves customers with a quiet frustration. The open position is on the other side of it. Dove didn't claim softer skin than rivals. It sided with customers against the category's own message.
Rivals selling flawless faces couldn't easily follow without contradicting their own ads.
cards.softwareNote: If every tool in your market promises more features and more notifications, the blind spot may be users who feel overwhelmed. A product positioned on doing less, calmly, can own a place the feature race can't reach.

cards.title: Why the position worked for Dove.
body: A bold stance alone isn't enough. Several things lined up:
list: **The gap was real:** research, not a hunch, pointed to it
**It fit the product:** Dove sold everyday soap and lotion, never glamour
**It was hard to copy:** rivals' whole image rested on the ideal Dove questioned
**It invited talk:** debate meant free reach in press and online
cards.callout: A position works when it's true, fits what you sell, and costs rivals something to copy.

cards.title: A stance is a promise you must keep.
body: Critics noted that Unilever also sold Axe (Lynx) with ads that treated women as objects, and a skin-lightening cream, Fair & Lovely, renamed Glow & Lovely in 2020. Others asked how a brand selling firming lotion could fight beauty pressure.
In 2017, a short Dove body-wash ad on Facebook was widely criticized as racist, and Dove apologized.
Ordinary brands survive a weak ad. A brand that claims to be on the customer's side pays more for every slip.

cards.title: Now it's a home repair company.
body: You run a plumbing and repair service. Every competitor's ad says the same thing: *fast, reliable, 24/7*. Your reviews and calls show customers mostly dread surprise bills and feeling talked down to.
Which position should you take?

options.text: Advertise that you're the fastest in town
options.feedback: It joins the crowded spot everyone already claims. You'd compete on a promise customers can't check until it's too late.

options.text: Price agreed before work starts, every step explained, old parts shown
options.feedback: It answers the frustration rivals ignore, and it's proven on every job. The cost: one surprise bill now hurts you more than anyone else.
Right gap, weak proof. A claim with no visible practice behind it sounds like every other ad.

cards.title: Find what every rival's promise leaves unsaid.
body: The strongest position is often the frustration your whole category created. Take it only if it's true and you can live by it.
**Try it today:** write down the one promise every competitor makes. Then write how that promise leaves customers feeling. Is anyone speaking to that?
